\chapter{Proposal Feedback and Iteration Plan}
\section{Proposal Feedback Summary}\label{ch3:sec:feedback}
The proposal was defended on 11 September 2026 and the decision was \textbf{Approved with Minor Modifications}. The panel wrote:
\begin{quote}
Approved. Do more research to improve your proposed solution and implement the given suggestions. \ldots{} students need to think more carefully about the proposed solution (e.g., in the case of a Flake Trace, how will the system detect it if no logs are available?). In the next presentation, students need to answer: 1) Will log trace instructions be injected into the code? 2) Will the code be modified? 3) How will the code block be isolated? 4) What are diverse scenarios where this approach is applicable?
\end{quote}
We turned each point into a numbered action, A1--A6, and added four actions, A7--A10, from sections 7--10 of the post-defence improvement and execution plan (\path{Mid Eval/FlakeTrace-Defense.pdf}). Every action has an owner, a decision, a status and an evidence link, kept in \path{docs/08-MidEval/panel-action-register.md} and updated whenever the work moved it.

\section{Iteration Strategy}\label{ch3:sec:strategy}
The project runs in four iterations (\path{docs/00-Meta/roadmap.md}): Iteration 1 from August to October, Iteration 2 from November to January, Iteration 3 from February to April and Iteration 4 in May and June. Each phase is judged by its \emph{exit evidence}, what must exist and be demonstrable at its end, not by the activities done in it. For FYP-1 the exit evidence is a working prototype from input to certificate with measured baselines; for the end of FYP-2 it is frozen results, a deployed release and a reproducibility bundle.

Within an iteration the work is split into small work packages, each with one owner. Three rules turn every package into evidence the supervisor can check:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Contracts first.} The three packages meet only through the contracts in \path{docs/contracts/}. A decision that affects more than one member becomes an ADR, accepted by all three before code is written against it (Section~\ref{ch5:sec:adrs}).
  \item \textbf{Branch, pull request, review.} Each package is built on its own branch and merged through a pull request that CI must pass and another member must approve (\path{CONTRIBUTING.md}). Each member commits their own work after reading the change.
  \item \textbf{Evidence with every change.} Anything run is recorded with its command and real result in the member's evidence log (\path{docs/evidence-m1.md}, \path{-m2.md}, \path{-m3.md}); no result is written down that was not produced by a run.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Iteration 1 Plan}\label{ch3:sec:it1}
Iteration 1's objective is stated in Section~\ref{ch6:sec:objectives}: diagnose order-dependent failures on a seeded fixture without logs, minimise the order, name the resource from bytecode, report a confidence interval, keep the source unchanged, and leave negative controls unresolved. The plan (\path{docs/08-MidEval/iteration-plan.md}) has fourteen work packages, W1--W14; Table~\ref{ch6:tab:wps} lists each with its owner and state.

The plan was set against the submission date S (Wednesday 14 October) and the meeting on Friday 16 October:
\begin{itemize}
  \item by 8--9 October: the fixture with pre-registered ground truth, the statistics, the outcome decision and the baseline interface (W1--W4, Member 3), and one repository with CI (W5, Member 2);
  \item by S$-$2: the order runner (W6, Member 2); by S$-$1: the static extractor (W8, Member 1), the diagnosis runs (W7, Member 2) and the end-to-end command (W9, Members 2 and 3);
  \item by S: minimisation for the two-polluter case (W10, Member 2), the report (W11) and the tag \texttt{mid-eval-v1} (W12); the day before the meeting, a rehearsed demonstration (W13).
\end{itemize}
The plan also fixed an \emph{emergency cut} in advance: if the submission came within two days, the demonstration would cover only F1 and N1, and F2, F3 and minimisation would be stated as in progress. It was not needed: all seven fixture cases run end to end (Chapter~6).

\section{Iteration 2 Plan}\label{ch3:sec:it2}
Iteration 2 runs from November to January. The roadmap commits it to resource normalisation and the test--resource graph, dynamic resource collection, search with ranking and an adaptive policy, the ablation harness, and deletion minimisation (\path{docs/00-Meta/roadmap.md}). Deletion minimisation is already built (Section~\ref{ch6:sec:ddmin}). The outcome fixed for the FYP-1 Final evaluation is: the primary scenario working end to end on all fixtures and on at least one real project from the benchmark manifest, and a first deployment attempt in a container (\path{iteration-plan.md}). The chapter ``Remaining FYP Plan'' gives the full plan for FYP-2.

\textbf{What Iteration 1 does instead of a container.} The runner already gives the isolation the fixture needs, and each part is in the code: every order runs in a fresh JVM, so no state survives between runs (\path{runner/order_runner.py}); a run longer than 120\,s is stopped and reported as \texttt{flaketrace.Timeout}, and a JVM that exits early is reported as \texttt{flaketrace.JvmCrash}, so a misbehaving test can neither hang the diagnosis nor vanish from it; processes are started from argument lists, never through a shell; every project file except \path{target/} and \path{.git/} is hashed with SHA-256 before and after, and any change forces \texttt{UNRESOLVED(SOURCE\_INTEGRITY\_FAILED)} (\path{runner/integrity.py}); and the record folder may not be inside the project (\path{runner/diagnose.py}). What it does not give is isolation of the file system, the network or resources from the analysed tests; that is the container's job, which is why FlakeTrace is for trusted projects until then (Section~\ref{ch9:sec:security}).

Two Mid items are not late but not yet done: the rehearsed demonstration (due the day before the meeting) and the tag \texttt{mid-eval-v1} (due with the submission on 14 October). Both are tracked as W12 and W13 (Table~\ref{ch6:tab:wps}).
